props.title: Restoration
props.initialSlug: Medical drama in Charles II's England

sections.content: Restoration exemplifies the lavish period drama wave of the 1990s, joining ranks with The Madness of King George (1994) and Rob Roy (1995) in bringing 17th-century England to vivid life. Robert Downey Jr. delivers one of his most underappreciated performances as Robert Merivel, a hedonistic physician in Charles II's court who falls from grace and finds redemption. The film's stunning Oscar-winning production design and costumes create an immersive portrait of Restoration England, from opulent palace interiors to plague-ravaged London streets.

sections.content: The film's themes of medical ethics and personal redemption echo through other period medical dramas like The Elephant Man (1980) and Mary Reilly (1996). Director Michael Hoffman balances the decadent spectacle of the Restoration court with intimate character study, while Hugh Grant delivers a commanding performance as King Charles II that predates his romantic comedy typecasting.

The 1990s saw a renaissance of British historical dramas, with Elizabeth (1998) and Shakespeare in Love (1998) following Restoration's lead in combining historical accuracy with contemporary psychological complexity. The film's exploration of science versus faith during the dawn of modern medicine parallels similar themes in The Physician (2013) and Perfume: The Story of a Murderer (2006). sections.content: Restoration particularly excels in its depiction of 17th-century medicine, showing both the superstitions of the time and the emergence of scientific method. This attention to medical historical detail can be seen in later films like Anonymous (2011) and The Royal Physician's Visit (2012), though few match Restoration's commitment to showing the brutal realities of medieval medical practice alongside court intrigue.
